In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of environmental variability on the genetic structure of a subdivided population.
the effect of variable environments and subdivided populations on genetic variation at a single locus, with special emphasis on the effect of temporal variation on polymorphisms with several alleles.
the effects of temporal and spatial variation in the environment on genetic polymorphisms in subdivided populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, if a population is subject to total panmixia, temporal variation in viabilities or both, the number of alleles at any locus will be at most two.

the only stable equilibria are fixation and the geometric mean of homozygote frequencies, and that these two equilibria are stable only when total panmixia or temporal environmental variation is operating.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for any number of alleles at a single, non-linked locus, a stable equilibrium state is assured for any selection regime that is submultiplicative, i.e. entails heterozygote viability greater than the geometric average of the corresponding homo- and heterozygote.

, with a few notable exceptions, the behaviour of a subdivided population is qualitatively similar to that of a panmictic population, but that, in some cases, the stable equilibrium of the subdivided population is unique.

, with the exception of the special case of two alleles and multiplicative viabilities, the effects of variable environments and subdivision on the polymorphic behaviour of a population at a single locus with several alleles are qualitatively the same as for two alleles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of several alleles is not a sufficient condition for the existence of multiple stable equilibria.
the presence of several alleles at a single autosomal locus does not necessarily lead to the evolution of polymorphism.
the stability of polymorphic equilibria is highly sensitive to environmental variation and the form of the viability function.
